bib.title: Experimentation in action: Moving from prototype to MVP (chapter 7 of Machine Learning Engineering in Action)

question: How should a prototype forecasting model be tuned and scaled so that it is robust enough for an MVP across thousands of airports?
contributions: Compares manual, grid, random, Bayesian (Hyperopt TPE) and autoML tuning and recommends model-based optimisation.
Shows Hyperopt on a Holt-Winters model, run serially, via SparkTrials on the driver, and via pandas_udf per group on workers, with MLflow logging of each trial.

results.claim: A full grid over the 11 Holt-Winters hyperparameters in the worked example has 32,768 combinations.
results.setup: Figure 7.3 grid over trend, seasonal, periods, dampening, smooth level and other options of the HWES model
results.note: Figure 7.3 labels the product as 32,768 though the displayed grid lists only some of the factors

results.claim: At 5 seconds per model, the 32,768-combination grid takes about 1.9 days serially.
results.setup: Assumes about 5 seconds per model iteration, serial

results.claim: Serial Hyperopt TPE tuning at 400 iterations per airport on a single-core VM took 3 hours 34 minutes for the four-airport example.
results.setup: Single-core VM, 400 Hyperopt iterations, serial loop over airports (EWR, JFK, LGA, SWF); figure label says '~1,600 models' (garbled in text)
results.note: The figure text reads 'we built ,600 models', so the model count is not recoverable from the text

results.claim: SparkTrials on a small four-node cluster cut the tuning phase from just over 3.5 hours to just under 30 minutes.
results.setup: Four-node Spark cluster, Hyperopt iterations raised to 600, parallelism 8, versus single-core VM at 400 iterations; no loss comparison printed
results.quote: from just over 3.5 hours to, on a relatively small four-node cluster, just under 30 minutes

results.claim: Projected: a 40-node cluster running one airport model per worker via pandas_udf would take about 23 hours for 7,000 airports.
results.setup: Extrapolation, not a reported run; comparators are a sequential VM loop (> 5,000 hours) and driver-side distributed tuning (> 800 hours)
results.quote: to 23 hours for all 7,000 airports, as opposed to either running them in a VM
results.note: The text says 'would' so this is an estimate

results.claim: Projected: sequential tuning of 7,000 airports in a VM loop would exceed 5,000 hours.
results.quote: a sequential loop-within-a-loop (> 5,000 hours), or collecting the data to the driver of

results.quote: a Spark cluster and running distributed tuning (> 800 hours)

results.claim: Rule of thumb: when raising Hyperopt parallelism, add iterations as single-core iterations + (parallelism / 0.2), so the TPE has enough prior results.
results.setup: Author's practice with Hyperopt SparkTrials; asynchronous trials lack in-flight results, pushing TPE toward random search; the author also says scaling iterations by the parallelism factor is not advisable

results.claim: Grid search spends equal trials on important and unimportant hyperparameters, so random search and TPE are preferred.
results.source: Bergstra and Bengio 2012, Random Search for Hyper-Parameter Optimization
results.setup: Cited in a sidebar; no numbers given

results.claim: Hyperopt TPE found a tuned JFK Holt-Winters model with smoothing_level 0.173, seasonal_periods 24 and trend add on the holdout.
results.setup: JFK total passengers, HWES, Hyperopt TPE; figure shows a backtest plot, no error value in the text
results.note: No loss number is printed for the tuned vs the untuned model

limits: Chapter is practitioner advice; the only timings are one author-run example, and the 7,000-airport hours are extrapolations.

No loss values are given to show that the parallel SparkTrials runs match serial tuning quality; the author only says 600 iterations at parallelism 8 were used 'to attempt to achieve similar loss metric performance'.
Claims that Hyperopt is 'nearly guaranteed to outperform even the most experienced DS' and that autoML is unsuitable for experienced teams are opinions without data.

Tooling has dated: pandas_udf with PandasUDFType.GROUPED_MAP, statsmodels 0.11.1, seaborn style 'seaborn', Hyperopt/Spark versions; the author says Optuna continues Hyperopt's work and the point of the book is process, not technology.
Spark serialization limit of 2 GB for collecting data to the driver is stated 'at the time of this writing'.
practices: Tune every model; never ship API defaults, since optimal values depend on algorithm, data and target (sidebar, start of chapter).
Avoid manual tuning except for algorithms with one or two Boolean or categorical hyperparameters, and abandon it once the prototype phase ends (section 7.1.1 tip).

Prefer random search to grid search, and prefer model-based optimisation (Hyperopt TPE) for large spaces; leave uninfluential hyperparameters in the TPE space since it weights influential ones (7.1.1, 7.1.3).
Avoid building your own autoML framework mid-project; it needs bandwidth, business approval and justified return (7.1.1).
Make previously hardcoded prototype values into tunable hyperparameters once TPE is used (7.1.3).
Wrap the per-model objective with functools.partial so only the hyperparameters vary between iterations, and collect Trials data and plots for later search-space refinement (7.1.3).
Log each Hyperopt trial as an MLflow child run under a parent run per entity, with searchable tags, params, metrics and plot artifacts, for provenance and comparison (7.2.2, 7.2.3).

Choose the parallelism axis by cost: distribute trials with SparkTrials, or distribute entities with a grouped pandas_udf and per-worker Trials(), which scales horizontally with workers (7.2.2, 7.2.3).
Do not call toPandas() on large Spark data; filter and loop in chunks (7.2.2 warning).
Use unique MLflow run names (airport, experiment name, uuid fragment, trial count) to avoid collisions in concurrent runs (Listing 7.9).
Filter out entities with too little history before modelling (Listing 7.11).
Pick the execution platform to minimise cost and risk and shorten the development cycle; break long monolithic jobs into restartable pieces (7.2.1, 7.2.4).

terms.definition: Open source package implementing the tree-structured Parzen estimator Bayesian optimisation from Bergstra et al.
Object recording the history of the optimisation runs so the algorithm can use prior results.
Tracking object that lets the cluster driver keep the history of experiments executed on remote workers, instead of the standard Trials object on one VM.
Dips and valleys between parameters and loss; if the search space is not explored sufficiently a model's tuning can sit in a local instead of the global minimum.
Spark function that takes grouped data as a pandas DataFrame via Apache Arrow and returns a pandas DataFrame, used to run an independent model fit per group on each worker.
Subject-matter experts who know business needs but lack the experience to hand-craft an ML solution; the target audience of autoML tools per the author.
